g.passage: Night makes people truthful. At the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I was the nurse who sat up with the patients who could not sleep, and Thorvald was the most stubborn of them. He would not lie down until I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where he watched the water as if a boat were due. On the fourth night he told me about his brother, a quarrel over their father's boathouse, and a letter he had written the week after and carried in his coat ever since. His brother had died the following spring. I said that someone in the family might still read the letter, and he shook his head. An apology, he said, was a door that opens from one side only. After that he spoke less and slept more. When he asked me, Sigrid, to burn the envelope in the ward stove, I did, and I noticed that he no longer looked out at the water.

g.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
On Forty-Third Street my father, Santiago,
kept every clock in the window five minutes fast
so passersby would think themselves late and hurry in.
Ottavio came in January with his wife's watch,
mainspring snapped, the crystal fogged like breath on glass.
He laid his nickels out in a careful row.
My father slid them back across the counter
and bent above the bench past closing, past supper,
lending the stranger his own evening,
asking nothing on account.
I translated nothing. Nothing needed saying.
When the small heart started, Ottavio wept in Italian;
my father answered him in Spanish.
Neither man asked when the debt would come due.
I stood between them holding my English,
the one who believed words were the price of things.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “lending the stranger his own evening” most nearly suggests that Santiago was

g.passage:
Once the library on Central Avenue was ours,
its radiators ticking like patient clocks,
Elan at the window with the paper folded small
while I, Nayeli, wandered the stacks.
We had a system: I chose, he signed,
and neither of us called it trust.
One Saturday in March, between the atlases,
he mentioned that the house was sold,
Denver by June, the papers settled.
Settled, I said, admiring the word
the way one admires a stranger's handwriting.
Now I notice that the radiators hiss.
I notice how the books lean on one another
like people who have never been introduced.
I check out a road map, sign for it myself,
and practice the signature until it looks like someone older.

g.passage: By the seventh evening of the rains, the people of the lane had made a song about Kwesi. Up the stairs he went to Obinna's projection booth, always with the same cracked lens bundled in a cloth, and down he came with the lens glued and the song a verse longer. Obinna, who mended everything in the old Accra cinema, from ceiling fans to torn reels, played his part well. He sighed loudly, rolled his eyes for the children watching from the steps, and glued. Glass is like a promise, he told them; mend it once and it remembers the break. On the seventh evening, though, he raised the lens into the projector's beam to test his work, and the picture on the screen below came apart into two faces, one bright and one faint. Obinna lowered the lens. The children on the steps stopped singing without being told. In a voice the lane had never heard him use, he asked Kwesi whose film had last passed through this glass, and when Kwesi answered, Obinna wrapped the lens in his own handkerchief.

g.passage: We found the letters in a biscuit tin under the workbench of our mother's radio shop in Marrakesh, a week after the funeral. Yiannis read them aloud while I, Yasmin, sorted vacuum tubes into egg cartons. Each was from a man who signed with a single initial, thanking her for another repair she had refused to charge for, month after month, for eleven years. My brother set the last one down and looked at me, and I knew the word he was not saying. __She had always closed the shop an hour early on Thursdays, and she had never once told us where she went.__ For a while neither of us spoke. Then Yiannis turned the tin over, and a pamphlet slid out from beneath the paper lining: a schedule of Thursday evening readings at a school for the blind, with our mother listed as the volunteer who kept its radios working. The same initial was printed beside the director's name. Outside, the call to prayer rose over the rooftops, and Yiannis began, very carefully, to put the letters back in order.

g.passage: On the first Tuesday of each month, I fetched my younger brother Wolfram from a reading room near the Ringstrasse in Vienna, where his tutor, Anselm, taught him geography from maps older than our grandparents. Anselm was always late, he hummed while he corrected, and he would not let Wolfram use the tram diagram I had copied out for him. A boy should know a city by its faces, he said, its domes and fountains and shop signs, not by its numbered lines. I told my mother this was an old man's vanity. In February the trams stopped for two days in a snowstorm, and I went out in a panic and found Wolfram already halfway home, steering past the green church dome, the bakery's brass pretzel, the fountain with the chipped nose. I said nothing to Anselm about it the next Tuesday. He was late again, and humming. But I waited for him in the reading room instead of the cold hall, and on the walk home I let Wolfram choose the way.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Anselm?
options: Lasting suspicion, since she still doubts that his methods kept Wolfram safe
Open gratitude, since she thanks him warmly for preparing Wolfram so well
Grudging respect, shown more in her actions than in anything she tells him
Weary tolerance, since his lateness and humming still outweigh his lessons
g.explanation: 화자는 처음에 Anselm의 지도법을 노인의 허영이라 여겼지만, 눈보라 속에서 Wolfram이 그가 가르친 랜드마크로 길을 찾는 것을 본다. 그 뒤 그녀는 Anselm에게 아무 말도 하지 않으면서도 추운 복도 대신 열람실에서 기다리고 동생에게 길을 고르게 하는 행동으로 인정을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. D는 Anselm이 여전히 늦고 흥얼거린다는 서술에 끌린 그럴듯한 오답이지만, 화자의 행동 변화를 설명하지 못한다. B는 그녀가 아무 말도 하지 않았다는 점과, A는 눈보라 장면의 결과와 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: Who should stay behind when the olives go down to market? So begin the tellers on the terraces above Naples, and so began young Emilio, newly sent to the hill school, who answered the question with great confidence. The slowest reader, he declared, would stay to mind the trees. Alessia read slowly and counted faster than the priest. She folded her arms and stayed. By noon the baskets at market were tallied wrong, the prices tangled, and Emilio was climbing back up the hill with his collar undone, a climb the tellers describe at length and with evident pleasure. They are careful to add that he asked Alessia's pardon before he asked her help, and that the following year he chose by drawing lots. Some insist he never admitted the error aloud; others say he admitted it only to the trees. Grandmothers telling it still pause here to slice the bread.

g.passage: On the Thursday after the funeral, Josiah carried his late teacher's violin into the laundromat because he had nowhere else to wait while his shirts dried. Harriet, who conducted the youth orchestra, was folding towels two machines away. Everyone had assumed the old man would leave the instrument to her, his oldest student, not to a fourteen-year-old who still rushed his scales. Josiah offered to give it to her. Harriet looked at the dented case, then asked him to play something. She listened through two cycles of the dryers without correcting a note, and afterward she wrote down the name of a shop that restrings old violins cheaply. g.passage: Oaxaca was dry that March, and the river below my grandmother's village had shrunk to stones and cracked mud. Halfway across, Esperanza stopped and asked me to say my whole name. I said Eulalio, the name on my school papers. She waited, so I added the second one, which my parents had written on my birth record and never used. She asked me to say it again, louder, and then again. Years later I learned it had been her younger brother's, lost at this crossing in a high-water season, and that she was the last in the village who still spoke it. g.passage:
"Translate only what I say," Somchai told me the first morning, and so I have, Mother, for six weeks in this printing room in Chiang Mai. Yesterday the investors asked who had designed the new press. Somchai glanced at the young mechanic oiling the rollers and said the design was his own. I had seen the mechanic's drawings pinned above his bench, and for a moment I nearly said so. I translated Somchai's claim word for word. My face burned the whole afternoon. This morning the presses started early, and the room smells of ink and wet paper. Please send the recipe for the mango rice.

Mai

g.passage: I, Faris, found the letters on our third day snowed into the cabin above Beirut, tucked under the lining of my grandfather's desk drawer. Every one was addressed to Noor, his oldest friend, who was waiting out the storm with us, and none had been sent. In them he admitted that a prize-winning poem from their student years had been hers, not his. Noor sat knitting by the stove. Twice that week I had heard her remark that my grandfather never once apologized for anything, and both times she laughed as if it did not matter. That evening I set the bundle in her lap without a word. She read the first page and stopped knitting. Later we melted snow for tea, and the kettle took forever.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Faris most likely give the letters to Noor?
options: He wants to shame his grandfather's memory by revealing his dishonesty.
He hopes the letters will distract Noor from the long, dull snowstorm.
He thinks Noor should receive the apology she believed never came.
He wants to find out whether Noor had suspected the truth about the poem.
g.explanation: 편지들은 모두 Noor에게 쓰였지만 부쳐지지 않았고, 할아버지가 그녀의 시를 자기 것으로 삼았음을 고백하는 내용이다. 또 Noor가 할아버지는 한 번도 사과한 적이 없다고 웃으며 말하는 것을 Faris가 두 번 들었다는 단서를 이어 읽으면, 그녀가 받지 못한 사과를 전해 주려 했다는 C가 정답이다. A는 고백 내용에서 다른 감정을 끌어낸 오답이고, D는 Noor가 읽고 뜨개질을 멈춘 결과를 동기로 착각한 것이다. B는 눈보라라는 소재만 빌린 외부 이유다.
